paragraphs.text: Bridges have been central to life along the River Tyne in the north-east of England since the second century AD, when the Roman settlement of Pons Aelius was established at the site now occupied by Newcastle-upon-Tyne's medieval Castle Keep. Aelius was the surname of the emperor Hadrian, and the settlement was the only one outside Rome named after an emperor, indicating a particular importance.

The original bridge over the River Tyne was built by the Romans on the site of the present-day Swing Bridge over the river. Not just a crucial part of Roman infrastructure, the bridge at Pons Aelius was also a place of worship. Two altars, dedicated to the water gods Neptune and Oceanus, were found on the site of the bridge in the late 19th century. It would appear that, from the beginning, the bridge was entwined with the identity and culture of the local population.

Over the centuries, more bridges were built across the River Tyne. By the 1920s, the enormous expansion in road traffic meant that a new crossing over the river joining the city of Newcastle with nearby Gateshead was vital. The solution was to build a new high-level road bridge to connect with the existing main road from London to Scotland, carrying traffic across the river without having to descend to river level. Work began in August 1925, to a design by the engineering firm of Mott, Hay and Anderson – designers of the strikingly similar Harbour Bridge in Sydney. Contrary to local myth, this new Tyne Bridge did not inspire the Harbour Bridge. Although the Australian landmark only opened in 1932, four years after the Tyne Bridge, its design had been approved in 1924 – a year before the Tyne Bridge project was begun. It is thought, though, that Mott, Hay and Anderson used the Tyne Bridge as a trial run for their ideas.

For the people of Gateshead, construction of the Tyne Bridge resulted in the loss of their commercial and industrial centre. Bottle Bank, a steep, busy street that swept down to the River Tyne, was largely destroyed to clear the way for construction. But although the bridge came at a cost to the local community, it was also a beacon of hope during troubled economic times, and was proposed as a method of bringing down unemployment among skilled workers in the area. Constructing the bridge was to provide livelihoods for those facing an uncertain future. The method used to weld bridge panels together was very similar to that used to build a ship, the industry for which the area had previously been well known. Therefore it was possible to use workers' existing skills. The arch of the bridge was erected by construction teams working simultaneously from each side of the river using cables, cradles and cranes, in what is thought to be the first use of such a construction technique in the UK. When completed, the bridge was immediately celebrated as a symbol of the region's reputation for industrial excellence – and a source of considerable local pride.

On October 10, 1928, tens of thousands of citizens of Newcastle and Gateshead lined the streets as King George V officially opened the Tyne Bridge. The crowds included 2,000 local school children, each presented with a brochure to commemorate the occasion. In the 90 years since the royals made that initial crossing in their carriage, the bridge has become an internationally recognised symbol of Newcastle, and of the north-east of England.

The iconic arch of the bridge, which is 162 metres in length from the base of one pier (a tower-like structure) to the base of the other, consists of arched steel ribs, connected by a system of diagonal shapes. The arch rises 55 metres above the level of the base of the piers, and 59 metres above the river when it's at high tide. The deck on which traffic travels is 26 metres above the high-water level, and 17 metres wide. The two piers were intended to provide space for a warehouse at either side of the bridge, but the inner floors were never built, so the piers have remained unused.

The bridge was originally named New Tyne Bridge, although whether this was to distinguish it from the Old Tyne Bridge, a medieval construction that was mostly destroyed by floods in 1771, or simply because at the time of its construction it was the new bridge over the Tyne, is not clear. Nowadays it is known simply as the Tyne Bridge.

In the late 20th century, the landscape of the north-east became closely associated with post-industrial decline, as shipyards, engineering firms and coal mines closed. Throughout this period, the Tyne Bridge stood firm as a symbol of the area's resilience and, more recently, of cultural regeneration. Since the turn of the 21st century, the mills, shipyards and markets that once lined the river banks have been replaced with restaurants, bars and world-renowned cultural centres.
